replacements.old_heading: X-COM Turns an Alien Invasion into a Problem of Budgets, Research and Fear
replacements.old_body: World UFO Day, observed on July 2, provides a concrete entry point into X-COM: UFO Defense. In the Mythos Games and MicroProse classic, UFOs are not merely enemies to shoot down: they are signals inside a global system of government funding, bases, interceptions, research and tactical missions. Every recovered alien technology changes future possibilities, while every loss affects personnel and politics. The result turns science-fiction imagery into a chain of decisions in which uncertainty is the real resource to manage.
replacements.heading: X-COM: defending Earth
replacements.body: UFO: Enemy Unknown (original title), also known as X-COM: UFO Defense in North America, is a 1994 science fiction strategy video game developed by Mythos Games and MicroProse. It was published by MicroProse for DOS and Amiga computers, the Amiga CD32 console, and the PlayStation. Originally planned by Julian Gollop as a sequel to Mythos Games' 1988 Laser Squad, the game mixes real-time management simulation with turn-based tactics. The player takes the role of commander of X-COM – an international paramilitary and scientific organisation secretly defending Earth from an alien invasion. Through the game, the player is tasked with issuing orders to individual X-COM troops in a series of turn-based tactical missions. At strategic scale, the player directs the research and development of new technologies, builds and expands X-COM's bases, manages the organisation's finances and personnel, and monitors and responds to UFO activity.

replacements.old_heading: Eco Makes the Environment a System That Reacts to Community Decisions
replacements.old_body: On June 5 World Environment Day draws attention to the collective effects of environmental choices. Eco, released in Early Access in 2018 by Strange Loop Games, turns that relationship into a shared simulation: extracting resources, producing energy, trading and building alter a persistent ecosystem. The problem is not only surviving a meteor but creating institutions and rules that can make progress coexist with ecological limits.
replacements.heading: Building a civilisation together
replacements.body: Eco is a simulation game created by American studio Strange Loop Games, in which players have to work together to create a civilization on a virtual planet. The game values a gentle use of natural resources and is used both as an entertainment and educational tool.

replacements.old_heading: When Coloring the World Means Taking Responsibility for It
replacements.old_body: UNESCO observes World Art Day on April 15, a date that finds an unusually concrete connection in Chicory: A Colorful Tale. The game imagines a world drained of color and gives the player a brush that can paint almost every surface. Creative action is not confined to an editor: it opens routes, solves puzzles, grows plants and changes relationships with inhabitants. Yet Chicory also uses that freedom to discuss expectation, creative block and artistic authority. The brush is both a desired power and a burden. That makes the game more interesting than a simple celebration of drawing: it turns making art into a mechanic that produces consequences, uncertainty and room for personal expression.
replacements.heading: A magical brush and a world without colour
replacements.body: Chicory: A Colorful Tale is an adventure video game by indie developer Greg Lobanov and published by Finji. It was released for Microsoft Windows, macOS, PlayStation 4, and PlayStation 5 in June 2021, for Nintendo Switch in December 2021, and for Xbox One and Xbox Series X and Series S in May 2023. The game features an anthropomorphic dog with a magical paintbrush, which is used to color the game world. Chicory: A Colorful Tale received "universal acclaim" from critics.

replacements.old_heading: From Sea to Plate, with Every Consequence in Between
replacements.old_body: The United Nations observes World Tuna Day on May 2 to highlight the economic and ecological importance of species central to global fisheries. DAVE THE DIVER offers a concrete connection because its daily loop joins diving, catching fish and serving them in a sushi restaurant. What Dave brings to the surface is not abstract loot: it becomes ingredient, revenue, menu and reason to return underwater. The game treats this system with a light tone and great variety, but it still makes visible a chain that videogames often split apart. Exploring the Blue Hole therefore means making decisions about oxygen, inventory, species and quantity; in the evening, those decisions return as dishes and restaurant economics.
replacements.heading: Diving by day, sushi by night
replacements.body: Dave the Diver is a 2023 video game developed and published by Mintrocket. The game combines both action-adventure and management gameplay styles as players explore deep sea environments to gather ingredients for a sushi restaurant. It was released for macOS and Windows in June 2023 following an early access release in October 2022.

replacements.old_heading: Seeing a Park at Bee Scale Changes the Meaning of Landscape
replacements.old_body: On May 20, FAO and the United Nations observe World Bee Day to highlight the role of pollinators. Bee Simulator provides a concrete video-game connection: it reduces the world to bee scale and turns flowers, wind, humans and routes into obstacles or resources. The game is not a complete scientific simulation, but it uses perspective to make an often invisible ecological job visible. Flying among plants shows that the same park becomes a completely different geography when the protagonist's body is only a few centimeters long.
